strengths: Significance: Online estimation of noisy low-rank tensors is a useful problem. The single-observation Riemannian update provides a unified approach to regression and completion while avoiding storage of the observation history.

Originality: The strongest contribution is the proposed use of spectral-projector expansions and martingale analysis to establish automatic incoherence preservation and entrywise error control (Theorems 5–6). This could provide valuable understanding beyond the algorithm itself.

Presentation: The manuscript provides explicit assumptions, algorithm pseudocode, and extensive derivations. Figure 1 illustrates the expected effects of step size and noise, with repeated trials for the noise-level comparisons.

Limitations and ethics: The manuscript explicitly acknowledges the warm-start requirement, its initialization cost, and unresolved initialization questions for binary completion. These disclosures are appropriate. No material ethical concern is apparent from the synthetic and public MovieLens experiments.
weaknesses: Soundness—martingale and expectation arguments: In Appendix D.1 (p. 49), the proposed martingale differences multiply centered quantities by an indicator depending on the current covariate; conditional centering therefore does not generally survive. More seriously, Appendix D.4 (pp. 79–80) uses an unconditional failure probability inside conditional Cauchy–Schwarz to obtain (91)–(92). Conditional on an iterate leaving the prescribed neighborhood, the relevant failure probability can be one. A valid stopping/truncation argument and control of contributions outside the neighborhood are needed to establish the central regret guarantees.

Soundness—adaptive regret: Theorem 8 specifies only an upper bound on the initial step size, allowing arbitrarily small steps and essentially no learning over a long interval. A matching lower bound or sufficient-contraction condition is necessary. Its proof (p. 82) also concludes E_k <= 2·4^(-k)·lambda_min^2 from a recurrence containing a positive noise term of order 2^(-k); that conclusion does not follow. The logarithmic-regret claim needs a corrected statement and proof.

Soundness—Poisson specialization: Theorem 4's proof (p. 18) bounds the Poisson variable's psi_1 norm by a quantity decreasing with intensity I. For Y distributed as Poisson(I), this norm equals 1/log(1+log(2)/I), which grows proportionally to I. Thus the stated noise bound and resulting intensity dependence are unjustified. The specialization also omits the signal-to-noise conditions required by its invocation of Theorem 1.

Soundness—missing initialization assumption: The binary-completion proof requires an initial row-norm/incoherence bound on U_0 (p. 77), but Theorem 6 assumes only rank and Frobenius proximity. Such proximity does not imply the required dimension-dependent row-norm bound. This missing hypothesis affects the claimed automatic preservation of incoherence.

Significance and originality claims need tighter support: The reduced completion sample complexity is conditional on a warm start whose construction still requires approximately d^(m/2) observations. The regret analysis concerns stationary stochastic prediction against the population truth. On p. 27, summing separate per-time minimax estimation rates does not itself establish a cumulative minimax regret lower bound with a common worst-case parameter. The broad claim of the first logarithmic regret in high-dimensional online learning also needs substantially stronger comparison with existing sparse online regression results.

Evaluation and reproducibility: Experiments cover linear regression/completion, with regret evaluated only for matrices; the generalized-linear claims receive no empirical assessment. No runtime or peak-memory measurements substantiate the practical efficiency claims. Initialization sample counts, adaptive schedule parameters, MovieLens preprocessing and tuning, and executable code are not supplied, preventing faithful reproduction of important results.

Presentation contains consequential inconsistencies: Contribution (f), p. 8, says adaptive statistical optimality and optimal regret cannot hold simultaneously, whereas Section 7 says they can. The alternative regret definition on p. 23 incorrectly takes an infimum of learner loss minus comparator loss. The O(1) storage claim on p. 20 excludes the model's required parameter storage. These issues make the scope and interpretation of the guarantees harder to assess.
